rationale: B wins because it finds the live danger in the update: "Hims & Hers won't say where its compounded semaglutide comes from" is the angle a real pharmacy-regulation reporter would ask first. A is competent, but it leaves the biggest hole as an afterthought in "Who supplies the compounded semaglutide..." and burns a slot on "Priced out of branded weight-loss drugs..." without a patient, price, or outcome. B's proof demands and crisis-holding next step make it usable before a founder walks into a regulatory buzz saw.
gaps_in_A: It misses the strongest standalone story. "Who supplies the compounded semaglutide" appears only as an uncomfortable question, when the unnamed supply source is the first hard-news angle here.

It pads with overlapping market-risk angles: "A newly profitable Hims & Hers doubles down..." and "Freshly profitable Hims & Hers bets its next act..." are cousins wearing different jackets. Also, "doubles down" is on the slop blacklist.

"Priced out of branded weight-loss drugs, patients turn to compounded prescriptions instead" asserts patient behavior without a named patient, an actual price comparison, or evidence anyone has turned to Hims for this reason.

"betting personalization sells better than price" invents a strategic claim. The update says Hims added at-home blood testing to personalize treatment; it does not say personalization beats price as the selling point.
gaps_in_B: "ongoing FDA-versus-compounders dispute that is already being reported" is plausible, but it reaches outside the supplied update. Good instinct, sloppy sourcing boundary.
"before it, this was prescription-only telehealth" invents the prior product state. The facts say the lab-testing service is new; they do not say what Hims offered immediately before.
"putting compounded semaglutide at the center of a consumer offering" slightly overstates the fact pattern. The update supports a launch, not centrality to the business or product strategy.

It throws out the patient lane too cleanly. Refusing "Weight-loss patients share their results with Hims & Hers" is right, but a narrower affordability angle could survive if the founder can produce real prices and a real patient.
